title: Reservations in two countries
summary: MesaLista books tables at 2,000 restaurants in Mexico and Texas. Payments need transactions and favorites are written in both countries.

requirements.1: {{s1}} keeps payments in managed MySQL without leaving Mexico, with a copy in another fault domain that takes over on its own if the primary fails.
requirements.2: {{s2}} gives reporting a separate copy of the slot 1 primary so it does not slow it down, even if the copy runs a few seconds behind.
requirements.3: {{s3}} stores favorites: each country writes in milliseconds to its own region and both accept writes. The other region sees them later, because availability is preferred over consistency.
requirements.4: {{s4}} alerts the reporting team if the slot 2 copy falls more than 30 seconds behind the primary.
requirements.5: {{s5}} keeps the database password out of the code: the app requests it at startup and a rotation scheduled every 30 days, with your own function as the target, changes it.
requirements.6: The pilot restaurant's MySQL runs on its own premises; its payments are migrated to slot 1 before opening to all 2,000 restaurants.

s1.explanation: MySQL HeatWave with HA places the secondaries in other fault domains when the region has a single AD and, if the primary fails, promotes a secondary on its own with no data loss. Only the primary gives read and write access.

s2.explanation: HeatWave read replicas are read-only copies updated asynchronously that scale out reads; they can lag behind the primary, and that is measured by their lag metric.

s3.explanation: With Global Active Tables every region serves reads and writes with single-digit millisecond latency; replication between regions is asynchronous and replicated data is read with eventual consistency.

s4.explanation: The HeatWave read replica guide measures the lag with the read replica lag metric and lets you create alarms on it; the Monitoring alarm notifies the team when the metric goes over 30 seconds.

s5.explanation: OCI Vault stores the password as a secret and can rotate it on its own, for example every 30 days (P30D), when the target is Autonomous AI Database or a function. For MySQL, rotation needs that function of your own.
s5.hint_cue: with your own function as the target

oci-mysql-ha.s2: In HA only the primary gives read and write access; the secondaries do not serve the reports.

oci-mysql-read-replica.s1: A read replica is a read-only copy updated asynchronously to scale out reads; the one that takes the primary's place is an HA secondary.

oci-autonomous-db.s1: Autonomous AI Database is not a MySQL system: Data Guard creates a standby updated with the primary's changes, but the payments need managed MySQL.
oci-autonomous-db.s2: Autonomous AI Database with Data Guard is a different database; it is not a copy of the slot 1 MySQL.
oci-autonomous-db.s3: With Autonomous Data Guard the standby is continuously updated with the primary's changes: writes come through the primary, not through both regions.

oci-audit.s4: Audit records calls to the OCI public APIs as log events; the replica lag is a metric, and alarms on metrics belong to Monitoring.

oci-object-storage.s5: Object Storage stores objects inside buckets; the scheduled rotation with an interval and a target system described in the OCI Vault guide is an option of Vault secrets.
